posts.title: expensive if-else trees
posts.hook: Most "AI agents" in production are glorified switch statements with an LLM doing the routing.
posts.body:
Most "AI agents" in production are glorified switch statements with an LLM doing the routing.

I know because I've built both kinds.

The first version of my enrichment pipeline was exactly this. Claude deciding which API to call, then formatting the output. It looked impressive in a demo. It broke constantly in production because the LLM would hallucinate a branch that didn't exist.

The version that actually works? Deterministic routing with LLM intelligence at specific decision points. The agent doesn't decide IF to enrich a lead. It decides HOW to interpret ambiguous enrichment results.

There's a pattern here that matters: the companies getting value from agents are constraining them to narrow, high-leverage decisions. Not "run my whole workflow." More like "this company has 3 possible LinkedIn pages, which one is actually them?"

That's a real judgment call. That's where the model earns its tokens.

Everything else is just code. Regular, boring, reliable code.

The irony is that building it this way is faster too. You test the deterministic parts with unit tests and the LLM parts with evals. Trying to eval an entire agentic workflow end-to-end is a nightmare nobody talks about.
posts.cta: What's the narrowest, highest-leverage decision you've handed to an LLM in production?

inspired_by.author: Cassie Kozyrkov
inspired_by.summary: Hot take: most companies building 'AI agents' are actually building very expensive if/else trees with a GPT wrapper. Real agentic infrastructure requires memory, tool orchestration, failure recovery, and audit trails — not just chaining prompts. I've seen 6 enterprise pilots this month. Only 1 had all four. That's your moat if you're building in this space.

remixes.label: debugging-the-demo
remixes.hook: The demo worked perfectly. Production lasted 11 minutes.
remixes.body:
The demo worked perfectly. Production lasted 11 minutes.

I showed a client my AI enrichment agent. It watched a lead come in, picked the right data source, enriched the record, and routed it to the right sequence. Beautiful.

Then real data hit. A company name with an ampersand. A LinkedIn URL that redirected. A job title in Portuguese. The LLM tried to improvise its way through each one, and every improvisation created a new failure mode.

The fix wasn't making the LLM smarter. It was making the LLM's job smaller.

I stripped the agent down to one decision: given these 6 signals, which of 3 enrichment tiers does this lead belong in? Everything downstream is deterministic. The API calls, the formatting, the routing. All hardcoded paths.

The LLM went from making 14 decisions per lead to making 1. Errors dropped from daily to maybe once a week. And the one decision it still makes? It's actually good at it, because classification is what these models were born to do.

The pattern I keep seeing: builders hand LLMs the entire workflow when they should hand them the one judgment call that's genuinely hard to write rules for. Everything else should be code.
remixes.cta: What's the one decision in your pipeline that actually needs an LLM?

remixes.label: taxonomy-of-fake-agents
remixes.hook: There are 3 types of "AI agents" in the wild. Only one of them deserves the name.
remixes.body:
There are 3 types of "AI agents" in the wild. Only one of them deserves the name.

Type 1: Prompt chains. A sequence of LLM calls where each step is predetermined. The AI doesn't decide what to do next. You decided at build time. This is a script with expensive string processing.

Type 2: Router agents. An LLM picks from a menu of predefined actions. Better. But if your menu has 4 items and the LLM picks wrong 8% of the time, you've built a system that breaks on every 12th request. I shipped one of these. The hallucinated tool calls were creative, I'll give them that.

Type 3: Constrained autonomy. The LLM makes exactly one high-value judgment, like classifying intent or scoring relevance. Everything before and after is deterministic code. The model does what models are good at. The code does what code is good at.

I rebuilt my entire enrichment pipeline from Type 2 to Type 3. Same inputs, same outputs. Went from firefighting daily to checking logs weekly.

The industry is selling Type 1 and Type 2 as "agentic AI" because the word agent is worth a 3x multiplier on pricing pages. The actual engineering is about knowing where the LLM boundary should be.
remixes.cta: Which type are you building right now? Be honest.

posts.title: list-level personalization
posts.hook: I stopped personalizing emails. Reply rates went up.
posts.body:
I stopped personalizing emails. Reply rates went up.

Not because personalization doesn't work. Because I was personalizing the wrong layer.

Old workflow: pull 2,000 leads, run each through a personalization prompt, generate a unique first line per person. Cost: ~$40 in API calls, 3 hours of compute, and a bunch of outputs that read like "I noticed your company recently expanded to Austin, congrats!"

Nobody cares.

New workflow: build 15 hyper-targeted lists of ~130 people each. Same job title, same company stage, same pain signal. Write ONE great email per list that speaks directly to that signal.

"You're hiring 3 SDRs while your enrichment is still manual" hits different when it's actually true for everyone on the list.

The math works out better too. 15 emails to write and refine vs. 2,000 AI-generated first lines to QA. The per-list approach takes me 2 hours total and I can actually read every email before it sends.

Signal-based list building is the personalization. The email just has to not waste it.
posts.cta: How granular are your outbound lists right now? 5 segments? 50?

inspired_by.author: Vin Matano
inspired_by.summary: We 3x'd reply rates by stopping personalization at the email level and starting it at the list level. Most teams spend 80% of their time writing 'personalized' intros to the wrong people. We spent that time instead building a Clay waterfall that only surfaces accounts with 3+ buying signals active simultaneously. Fewer sends, more pipeline.

remixes.label: segment-not-personalize
remixes.hook: Your outbound personalization is probably costing you replies.
remixes.body:
Your outbound personalization is probably costing you replies.

Here's the math that changed my approach.

2,000 leads. Each one gets a custom first line generated by Claude. Cost: $40 in API calls, 3 hours of compute time. Output: 2,000 unique opening sentences that mostly say variations of "congrats on the new office" or "loved your recent post about leadership."

The recipients can smell it. Everyone's inbox is full of AI-generated first lines now. The signal that used to say "I researched you" now says "I ran you through a prompt."

So I flipped the model. Instead of personalizing each email, I personalized each list.

50 leads who all just posted a VP of Sales role. 30 leads who expanded into a new market this quarter. 40 leads using a competitor who just raised prices. Each list gets one message that speaks directly to their shared situation.

The first line isn't about them individually. It's about the moment they're all in. "You're hiring your first sales leader" hits harder than "I noticed you posted a VP Sales role on LinkedIn, congratulations."

Cost dropped from $40 to under $2. Reply rates went up 40%. Not because the emails were more personal. Because they were more relevant.
remixes.cta: How many segments are you running right now? If it's under 20, you're probably still spraying.

remixes.label: death-of-first-lines
remixes.hook: AI-generated first lines are the new "Hope this email finds you well."
remixes.body:
AI-generated first lines are the new "Hope this email finds you well."

Every SDR team discovered the same trick at the same time: scrape a prospect's LinkedIn, feed it to an LLM, generate a custom opening line. It worked for about 6 months. Then everyone started doing it, and now every inbox has three emails that open with "I saw your team just expanded to Austin" or "Loved your take on RevOps in your recent post."

The personalization arms race created a new kind of generic.

I was spending $40 per campaign on API calls to generate these. When I looked at the data, the personalized campaigns and the non-personalized campaigns had nearly identical reply rates. The variable that actually moved the needle wasn't the first line. It was list quality.

A tight list of 50 people who all share the same trigger event, written to with one message that nails their exact situation, outperforms 2,000 individually personalized emails every time.

The work moved upstream. Instead of spending 3 hours generating unique first lines, I spend that time building narrow signal-based lists. Finding the 50 companies that just lost their VP of Marketing. The 40 that are running job ads for a role they didn't have last quarter.

The personalization lives in the list, not the copy.

posts.title: evals are the bottleneck
posts.hook: The bottleneck in AI products isn't the model. It's knowing whether the model did a good job.
posts.body:
The bottleneck in AI products isn't the model. It's knowing whether the model did a good job.

I run a content pipeline where Claude drafts LinkedIn posts, Reddit comments, and email copy. The generation takes seconds. Evaluating whether the output matches my voice, doesn't contain slop patterns, and actually says something worth reading? That's where all the time goes.

I built a 29-pattern detection system just for anti-slop. Things like em-dash overuse, authority signaling phrases, dramatic three-sentence parallel structures. Each one is a binary check. That part's easy.

The hard eval is "does this sound like a person wrote it with a specific point of view?" That's not a checklist. That's judgment. And right now the best eval for that is... me reading it.

This is the unsexy part of building with AI that nobody posts about. You can ship the v1 in a weekend. Then you spend months building the evaluation layer that makes the output consistently good enough to trust.

Every AI-native team I talk to hits this same wall around month 3. The model works. You just can't tell when it doesn't.
posts.cta: What's your eval setup? Vibes-based, rubric-based, or LLM-as-judge?

inspired_by.author: Lenny Rachitsky
inspired_by.summary: Just ran a survey of 400 PMs at AI-native companies. 67% say their #1 bottleneck is NOT the model — it's evaluation pipelines. They can't tell if their agent is getting better or worse between deploys. The teams winning are the ones who've built robust evals first, then iterated the model. Build your evals before you build your product.

remixes.label: eval-stack-walkthrough
remixes.hook: I spent 2 hours building my AI content generator. I've spent 2 months building the system that tells me if the content is any good.
remixes.body:
I spent 2 hours building my AI content generator. I've spent 2 months building the system that tells me if the content is any good.

The generation part is trivial at this point. Claude can draft a LinkedIn post in 4 seconds. A Reddit comment in 2. An email in 6. The prompts took a few iterations, but they're stable now.

The eval layer is a different beast entirely.

First, I built a 29-pattern slop detector. Things like "Here's the thing" openers, em dash overuse, sycophantic framing, hollow CTAs. If a draft trips 3 or more patterns, it gets flagged for rewrite, not patch. You can't fix slop with find-and-replace.

Then I added voice matching. I have a reference corpus of my actual writing. The eval checks whether the draft sounds like me or sounds like "helpful AI assistant." This catches the subtle stuff: the cadence, the sentence length distribution, whether it uses specifics or hides behind abstractions.

Finally, a substance check. Does the post contain at least 2 of these: a specific example, a technical detail, visible reasoning, a concrete result, or a genuine gotcha? If not, it's filler dressed up as insight.

All three layers run before I ever see the output. Most drafts fail the first pass. That's the point. The eval is the product. The generator is commodity.
remixes.cta: What percentage of your AI outputs do you actually review before they ship?

remixes.label: vibes-to-rubrics
remixes.hook: "Does this sound right?" is not an eval strategy. It's a prayer.
remixes.body:
"Does this sound right?" is not an eval strategy. It's a prayer.

I ran on vibes for months. Claude would generate content, I'd read it, I'd think "yeah, that works" or "nah, rewrite." The problem is that vibes don't scale, vibes don't teach the system anything, and vibes shift based on whether I've had coffee.

So I started writing down what I was actually checking for.

Every time I rejected a draft, I asked myself: what specifically is wrong? Not "it doesn't feel right." What pattern triggered the rejection? I cataloged 29 of them. Hollow openers. Fake specificity. The "here's why this matters" bridge that adds no information. Lists that could be in any order.

Then I turned each pattern into a detection rule. Some are regex. Some are structural checks. A few need an LLM pass. The system runs all 29 against every draft before it reaches me.

The shift from vibes to rubrics did three things. It cut my review time by 60% because the obvious failures never reach me. It gave Claude actionable feedback so rewrites actually improve. And it forced me to articulate what "good" means in my voice, which is knowledge I didn't have until I built the eval.

The eval didn't just measure quality. Building it improved my understanding of what quality means.
remixes.cta: Have you ever written down what specifically makes you reject an AI output?

posts.title: revops is data architecture now
posts.hook: Your CRM isn't your source of truth anymore. Your warehouse is. And most RevOps teams haven't caught up.
posts.body:
Your CRM isn't your source of truth anymore. Your warehouse is. And most RevOps teams haven't caught up.

I watch GTM teams spend weeks getting Salesforce fields right while their actual decision-making data lives in 4 spreadsheets, a Clay table, and someone's Notion.

The teams that move fast made a different choice: SQLite or Postgres is the brain. The CRM is a display layer.

My setup: every enrichment result, every signal, every score lands in a local database first. Attio gets a clean, reconciled view pushed to it. Not the other way around.

Why this matters: when you want to ask "which accounts showed hiring intent AND visited pricing AND match our ICP score threshold," you write a SQL query. You don't click through 6 Salesforce report filters and pray the data is current.

The architecture decision that determines your GTM speed isn't which CRM you pick. It's where computation happens. If your enrichment, scoring, and routing logic lives inside your CRM's automation builder, you've already lost flexibility.

Put the logic in code. Put the results in the CRM. That's the split.
posts.cta: Where does your GTM computation actually happen right now?

inspired_by.author: Dannie Herzberg
inspired_by.summary: RevOps in 2026 is less about Salesforce hygiene and more about data architecture decisions that determine whether your GTM team can move fast or not. I've seen $50M ARR companies paralyzed because their CRM schema was designed for a company half their size. The ops debt compounds silently until it doesn't. The best RevOps hires I've made were engineers who also understood how salespeople think.

remixes.label: crm-graveyard
remixes.hook: Your Salesforce is a graveyard of fields nobody updates and dashboards nobody trusts.
remixes.body:
Your Salesforce is a graveyard of fields nobody updates and dashboards nobody trusts.

I'm not being dramatic. I've worked with GTM teams that have 400+ custom fields in their CRM. Ask the VP of Sales where their pipeline data actually comes from and they'll point to a Google Sheet that an analyst updates every Monday morning.

The CRM became a compliance layer, not a decision-making tool. Reps update it because they have to, not because it helps them sell.

The teams I've seen break out of this pattern did something counterintuitive. They stopped trying to fix the CRM. Instead, they built a lightweight data layer underneath it.

posts.title: inference costs and building
posts.hook: Inference costs dropped 90% in 18 months. Most builders are still architecting like it's expensive.
posts.body:
Inference costs dropped 90% in 18 months. Most builders are still architecting like it's expensive.

I catch myself doing this constantly. Batching requests to minimize API calls. Caching aggressively. Building elaborate prompt chains to avoid a second LLM call.

Some of that is just good engineering. But some of it is leftover scarcity thinking from when a single Opus call cost $0.15.

The shift I'm making: instead of one careful prompt that tries to do everything, I'm running multiple cheap passes. First pass: rough draft. Second pass: anti-slop scan. Third pass: voice match scoring. Total cost per piece of content is about $0.03.

A year ago that same workflow would've cost $0.40 and I'd have built it as one mega-prompt to save money.

This changes the build calculus for solo founders especially. The "can I afford to run this at scale" question has a different answer now. The thing that costs real money isn't the model. It's the data you feed it and the infra you run it on.

If you're still optimizing for fewer LLM calls, check the pricing page again. The math probably changed since you last looked.

I rebuilt a pipeline last week and realized halfway through that I was optimizing for a constraint that no longer exists.

The pipeline batches 200 leads at a time, waits for the batch to complete, then processes results. I built it this way because 8 months ago, running 200 individual Opus calls would have cost $30 and taken 20 minutes.

Today the same 200 calls cost $3 and finish in under 2 minutes.

But I was still batching. Still caching. Still building elaborate prompt chains where one long call does the work of three shorter ones, because three calls felt expensive.

I ripped out the batching logic and let each lead run independently. The code got simpler. The error handling got simpler. When one lead fails, it doesn't hold up the other 199.

This is happening everywhere in AI engineering right now. We're carrying architectural debt from 2024 pricing into 2026 systems. Caching layers that cost more to maintain than the API calls they save. Prompt chains designed to minimize round trips when round trips now cost fractions of a cent.

The question I'm asking on every new build: what would this look like if I assumed inference was basically free? Not literally free. But cheap enough that optimizing for fewer calls is no longer the right trade-off.

The answer usually involves simpler code, more LLM calls, and better results. Because the best prompt is often three focused prompts, not one overloaded one.

remixes.label: three-calls-not-one
remixes.hook: Stop cramming everything into one prompt. Inference is cheap now. Use three calls instead.
remixes.body:
Stop cramming everything into one prompt. Inference is cheap now. Use three calls instead.

I spent months perfecting a single mega-prompt that extracted company info, scored fit, generated personalization, and drafted outreach. All in one Claude call. It was 2,000 tokens of instructions, carefully ordered to prevent the model from losing context.

It worked about 80% of the time. The other 20%, something in the middle would go wrong and corrupt everything downstream.

Last week I split it into three calls. Call 1: extract and structure the raw data. Call 2: score and classify. Call 3: generate the output using the clean, validated results from calls 1 and 2.

Each prompt is under 500 tokens. Each one does one thing well. If call 2 fails, I rerun call 2. The data from call 1 is fine.

Total cost increase: about $0.002 per lead. Total reliability increase: from 80% to 97%. Total code complexity decrease: I deleted 40 lines of error handling that existed only because the mega-prompt would fail in unpredictable ways.

The old mental model was "minimize API calls." The new mental model is "minimize the blast radius of any single failure." When calls are cheap, the correct architecture is lots of small, focused calls with validation between each step.

This applies to agents, enrichment pipelines, content generation, anything touching an LLM in production.

posts.title: replacing a hire with a workflow
posts.hook: I didn't replace a $180k hire with AI. I replaced the job description with a better architecture.
posts.body:
I didn't replace a $180k hire with AI. I replaced the job description with a better architecture.

The framing of "AI replaces people" misses what's actually happening. When I build an enrichment pipeline with Claude Code, I'm not doing what a data ops person would do, but faster. I'm doing something different entirely.

A person would log into 5 tools, copy-paste between tabs, make judgment calls in their head, and update a spreadsheet. My pipeline hits APIs directly, runs scoring logic in SQL, and pushes clean results to the CRM. No tabs. No copy-paste. No spreadsheet.

That's not the same job done cheaper. That's a different job.

The real question isn't "can AI do this person's work?" It's "if I designed this workflow from scratch today, knowing what tools exist, would I design it as a person sitting at a computer?"

Usually the answer is no. You'd design it as a script that runs on a schedule, with human review at specific decision points.

The people who thrive in this environment aren't being replaced. They're the ones designing the new workflows. The skill isn't operating tools anymore. It's architecting systems.

The $180k I "saved" was never about replacing a person. It was about realizing the job description was a symptom of missing infrastructure.

Most roles that feel essential are actually compensating for systems that don't talk to each other. Fix the architecture and the role dissolves on its own.

posts.title: content strategy vs seo strategy
posts.hook: 90% of B2B content strategies are just keyword lists with a publishing calendar.
posts.body:
90% of B2B content strategies are just keyword lists with a publishing calendar.

I know because I built one of those. Wrote 40 blog posts targeting long-tail keywords. Got traffic. Got zero pipeline from it.

The problem: the people searching those keywords were looking for information, not solutions. They'd read the post, get what they needed, and leave. Great for SEO metrics. Useless for revenue.

What actually moves pipeline for me now: writing about the specific problems I'm solving while building. Not optimized for search volume. Optimized for the 200 people who have the exact same problem and recognize themselves in the story.

One LinkedIn post about my enrichment pipeline architecture generated more inbound conversations than 6 months of SEO content. Because the people who cared were already on LinkedIn. They didn't need to Google it.

The content strategy that works: build in public on the platforms where your buyers already spend time. Let the blog be the long-form archive. Let social be the distribution engine. Let the specificity of your actual work be the filter.

Generic educational content attracts generic educational audiences. Specific build content attracts people who build.

inspired_by.summary: Hot take: most B2B content strategies are just SEO strategies with a LinkedIn distribution layer slapped on top. That's not a content strategy, that's a content calendar. Build for the dark funnel or keep wondering why your MQLs don't close.

remixes.label: traffic-trap
remixes.hook: I got 40,000 monthly visitors from SEO. My pipeline didn't notice.
remixes.body:
I got 40,000 monthly visitors from SEO. My pipeline didn't notice.

I spent six months building what I thought was a content strategy. Keyword research, content calendar, consistent publishing cadence. Textbook B2B playbook. The traffic charts looked beautiful. Up and to the right, every month.

Then I looked at where my actual deals were coming from. LinkedIn conversations. Podcast appearances. Direct referrals from people who'd seen me build in public. Not a single closed deal traced back to a blog post.

The blog visitors were researchers, not buyers. They wanted to learn about the topic. They got their answer and bounced. My content was serving the wrong audience with the wrong intent.

Here's what I do differently now. I write content that only makes sense if you're actively building something. Not "What is GTM engineering" but "Here's the exact pipeline I built this week and what broke." The traffic is lower. The DMs are higher.

Content strategy isn't about what you publish. It's about who you attract and what they do after reading. If your content attracts learners but you sell to builders, your strategy is a vanity metric in disguise.

The best content doesn't rank. It circulates.
remixes.cta: What's one piece of content you created that actually generated a real conversation?

remixes.hook: Your content strategy has a targeting problem disguised as a distribution problem.
remixes.body:
Your content strategy has a targeting problem disguised as a distribution problem.

Most B2B teams think their content isn't working because they need more reach. More keywords, more channels, more frequency. So they double down on production. Ship more posts, start a podcast, launch a newsletter.

But the issue isn't reach. It's intent mismatch.

I learned this by tracking where pipeline actually originates. Not where people first heard of me. Where the conversation started that led to a deal. Almost every time, it was a piece of content that demonstrated a specific capability. Not educational content. Proof-of-work content.

"How to build an outbound pipeline" attracts people researching the topic. "Here's the outbound pipeline I built for a client this week, including the parts that failed" attracts people who need that pipeline built.

Same topic. Completely different reader. One bookmarks your post. The other sends you a DM.

The fix isn't complicated. Stop writing for the person Googling the question. Start writing for the person who already knows the question and needs to see your answer in action.

SEO gets you an audience. Proof-of-work gets you pipeline. They're different strategies solving different problems.

posts.title: extended thinking changes agents
posts.hook: Extended thinking + tool use changed how I build agents overnight.
posts.body:
Extended thinking + tool use changed how I build agents overnight.

Before: my agents would call a tool, get a result, then immediately act on it. Fast, but dumb. They'd misinterpret ambiguous results and confidently do the wrong thing.

Now: the model actually reasons about the tool result before deciding what to do next. It'll pull enrichment data, notice something doesn't add up, and go verify before proceeding.

Real example from yesterday. My lead scoring agent pulled company data where the employee count said 12 but the LinkedIn page showed 200+ employees in the feed. Old agent would've scored it as SMB and moved on. New agent flagged the discrepancy, pulled a second source, and correctly identified it as a mid-market company with a stale data provider entry.

That's not a party trick. That's the difference between a pipeline full of mis-scored leads and one you can actually trust.

The practical takeaway: if you're building agents and haven't tested with extended thinking enabled, you're probably overengineering your prompt chains to compensate for reasoning the model can now do natively.

I deleted about 400 lines of "verification step" code this week. The model just... does it now.

Here's what changed. Before, the model would call an enrichment API, get back partial data, and confidently merge it into the record. Wrong name? Didn't notice. Conflicting signals? Picked one at random. My guardrails caught maybe 60% of these mistakes.

Now the model reasons about the result before acting. It sees partial data and decides to call a second source. It notices when a company name from one API doesn't match another and flags the conflict instead of silently overwriting.

The behavior I was building in code is now happening in the model's reasoning. Not perfectly. But well enough that my guardrails went from essential to redundant.

I deleted the output validators, the retry logic, the result classifiers. The agent got simpler and more reliable at the same time. That's the rare kind of improvement where less code means better results.

posts.title: ai sdrs expose the real problem
posts.hook: AI SDRs didn't kill the SDR role. They killed the "send 200 emails and pray" version of it.
posts.body:
AI SDRs didn't kill the SDR role. They killed the "send 200 emails and pray" version of it.

I've built outbound systems on both sides of this. Manual prospecting at scale, and now automated signal-based pipelines. The difference isn't speed. It's what you spend your time on.

When the machine handles list building, enrichment, and initial outreach, the human SDR's job changes completely. You're not grinding through ZoomInfo exports. You're analyzing which signals actually correlate with closed deals. You're writing the templates that convert. You're on calls with prospects who already engaged.

That's a harder job, not an easier one. And it requires a completely different skillset.

The SDRs I see thriving right now understand data. They can look at a signal report and say "this hiring pattern means they're 6 months from needing us." They think in systems, not sequences.

The ones struggling? They were always just doing volume. High activity, low thought. The AI exposed that the activity itself was never the valuable part.

The role isn't going away. The floor is going up. And that's probably a good thing for everyone still in the seat.

The SDR who sends 200 emails a day and the SDR who sends 20 aren't doing the same job.

I've managed both types. The volume SDR lives in a spreadsheet. Download list, load into sequence, hit send, pray for 2% reply rate. Success metric: activity count. It works through brute force and it scales linearly with headcount.

The signal SDR lives in context. They know which accounts just raised funding, which ones posted a job that matches your ICP trigger, which prospect just engaged with three pieces of content in a week. They send fewer messages because each one references something specific and timely.

AI didn't create this distinction. It just made the volume approach obviously inferior.

When machines handle list building, enrichment, sequencing, and initial outreach, the human SDR doing those things manually is competing against software. That's a losing position. But the SDR who can read signals, build context, and have real conversations? The machine can't do that yet.

The role isn't dying. It's splitting. Volume work goes to automation. Signal reading, relationship building, and creative outreach stay human. The SDRs who thrive in the next two years will be the ones who stopped measuring their output in emails sent and started measuring it in conversations started.

remixes.body:
We stopped hiring SDRs who are good at sending emails. We started hiring SDRs who are good at reading rooms.

The old SDR interview: "Walk me through your prospecting workflow. How many touches per day? What's your sequence cadence?" Every answer was about process execution. Could you follow the playbook at scale?

That entire interview is obsolete. A Claude Code script follows the playbook better than any human. It builds lists faster, enriches more completely, and sends more consistently. If process execution is the job, the job is already automated.

Here's what we interview for now. Give the candidate a messy account with conflicting signals. A company that looks like the ICP on paper but has red flags in the details. See if they can synthesize context, identify the real opportunity, and articulate why this account is or isn't worth pursuing.

We also test conversational instincts. Hand them a cold reply that's ambiguous. Not clearly interested, not clearly a rejection. How do they respond? The best SDRs read between the lines and adapt. The average ones reach for a template.

The skills that matter now: pattern recognition, contextual judgment, conversational intelligence, and creative problem-solving. None of which show up on an activity dashboard. That's why most SDR teams are measuring the wrong things while wondering why AI is eating their pipeline.

posts.title: solo founder $10k MRR reality
posts.hook: The $10k MRR solo founder story always gets engagement. The part nobody posts is what $10k MRR actually feels like.
posts.body:
The $10k MRR solo founder story always gets engagement. The part nobody posts is what $10k MRR actually feels like.

I'm building Clearbox as a solo founder right now. No co-founder, no funding. Just me, Claude Code, and a SQLite database that runs the whole operation.

$10k MRR sounds like freedom. In practice it means you're simultaneously the engineer, the sales team, the support team, and the person who has to decide whether to fix the bug or write the blog post today.

The coding agent changed the math on what's possible alone. I can ship features, run enrichment pipelines, generate content, and manage outbound in a single day. A year ago that was a 4-person team's work.

But the thing that doesn't scale with AI is decision-making. Which feature matters most. Which customer segment to double down on. When to say no to a paying customer because they'd pull the product in the wrong direction.

That's the real bottleneck for solo founders. Not building speed. Not even distribution. It's the cognitive load of making every single decision yourself, all day, every day.

The founders who sustain aren't the fastest builders. They're the ones who figured out which decisions to make once and encode into systems.

Nobody posts the $10k MRR screenshot alongside the 14-hour Tuesday where you were the support team, the sales team, and the engineer simultaneously.

I'm at that stage right now with Clearbox. Solo founder, no funding, building with Claude Code and SQLite. The revenue is real. The freedom everyone imagines? Less real.

Here's what $10k MRR actually looks like on a random Wednesday. Wake up to a support ticket that needs a code fix, not a template response. Spend the morning debugging instead of building the feature that would actually grow revenue. Get a sales inquiry at noon, context-switch completely, do a demo. Realize at 3pm you haven't touched the roadmap. Ship a half-finished improvement at midnight because tomorrow has its own fires.

The solo founder advantage is real. No meetings, no alignment tax, no waiting for approval. I can go from idea to shipped in hours. But the disadvantage is that every function of the business competes for the same brain.

The thing that's kept me sane is ruthless automation. Not the fancy kind. The boring kind. Automated alerts so I catch issues before they become tickets. Automated onboarding so I'm not hand-holding every new user. Cron jobs that generate reports I'd otherwise build manually every week.

Each piece of automation doesn't save much. But collectively, they're the difference between sustainable and burning out by month six.

remixes.body:
At $10k MRR as a solo founder, your survival depends on one skill: knowing what not to do today.

Every morning I wake up with more work than I can finish. Bug reports, feature requests, sales conversations, content to create, infrastructure to maintain. All legitimate. All important. All competing for the same 10 productive hours.

The founders who burn out at this stage aren't the ones who work too hard. They're the ones who work on everything. A support ticket feels urgent so they fix it immediately. A sales lead comes in so they drop everything for the demo. A competitor ships a feature so they panic-build a response.

What I've learned building Clearbox: the leverage decision is the only decision that matters. Each morning I ask one question. What is the one thing I can do today that makes tomorrow easier? Sometimes it's a feature. Sometimes it's automation. Sometimes it's saying no to a customer request that would derail the week.

My entire operation runs on Claude Code and a SQLite database. Not because I'm making a statement about minimalism. Because every tool I add is a tool I have to maintain, and maintenance is the silent killer of solo founders.

The $10k MRR milestone isn't the achievement. Staying at $10k MRR without losing your mind while building toward $50k, that's the actual game. And it's a systems problem, not a hustle problem.
